notes:
Here are my verse-by-verse notes on Ezekiel 3, drawn from the sources I was able to access.

---

## Ezekiel 3 — Verse-by-Verse Commentary Notes

### v. 1 — "Son of man… eat what you find here. Eat this scroll, then go and speak to the house of Israel."

- **Traditional Reading:** The scroll was the one introduced in Ezekiel 2:9–10, written on both sides with "lamentations, mourning, and woe." The command to eat comes with a threefold charge: eat, go, speak. The eating symbolizes internalising God's Word before proclaiming it. Ezekiel cannot preach what he has not first digested. (Enduring Word: https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-3/; Precept Austin: https://www.preceptaustin.org/ezekiel_31-15)
- **Matthew Henry:** Ezekiel was to receive the truths of God as food for his soul and feed upon them by faith; then he would be strengthened. He must speak all that, and that only, which God spoke to him. (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/mhc/ezekiel/3.htm)
- **Catholic (Haydock):** By this eating of the book was signified the diligent attention and affection with which we are to receive and embrace the word of God, letting it sink into our interior by devout meditation. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/hcc/ezekiel-3.html)
- **Reformed (Ligonier):** The scroll contained "words of lamentation and mourning and woe" — a message of covenant curses. Hearing the Lord’s curse on sin is ultimately sweet for those of faith; only after hearing the curse are we ready for the sweet gospel of salvation. (https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/scroll-and-watchman)

### v. 2 — "So I opened my mouth, and He fed me the scroll."

- **Traditional Reading:** Ezekiel’s immediate obedience is highlighted. Unlike the rebellious house who refuse God's Word, Ezekiel opens his mouth in willing submission. Precept Austin calls this "immediate obedience" and notes that delayed obedience is really disobedience. (https://www.preceptaustin.org/ezekiel_31-15)
- **Vision vs. Reality:** Enduring Word (Guzik) notes the context is almost certainly a vision — a kind of "spiritual and divine virtual reality" — not a literal eating of a physical scroll. Yet the experience was entirely real and powered the prophet for years of ministry. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-3/)

### v. 3 — "Eat and fill your stomach with this scroll… So I ate, and it was as sweet as honey in my mouth."

- **Traditional Reading:** The sweetness is surprising because the scroll contained "lamentations, mourning, and woe" (2:10). It was sweet because it was God's Word. Psalm 119:103 is echoed: "How sweet are Your words to my taste." Ezekiel was not to merely sample God's revelation but to fill himself with it. (Enduring Word: https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-3/)
- **F. B. Meyer (quoted by Guzik):** "It is specially incumbent on those who have to go forth and speak, to open their mouths and eat the roll. There is no greater mistake than to suppose that, because we are constantly handling God’s Word for the purpose of teaching and exhorting others, we are therefore feeding on it for ourselves." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-3/)
- **Precept Austin:** In every act of obedience there is a sweet taste. Obedience guarantees no freedom from pain, but it brings the satisfaction of a life pleasing to God. The same scroll that would taste bitter to the house of Israel tasted sweet on the prophet’s tongue. (https://www.preceptaustin.org/ezekiel_31-15)
- **Catholic (Haydock):** He readily accepted the commission but soon found the difficulties to which it would expose him. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/hcc/ezekiel-3.html)

### vv. 4–6 — "Go now to the house of Israel… not to a people of unfamiliar speech… Surely if I had sent you to them, they would have listened to you."

- **Traditional Reading:** Ezekiel is sent to his own people, not to Gentiles. The irony is sharp: if he were sent to foreigners whose language he could not understand, they would have listened. The problem with Israel is not linguistic or intellectual but moral — a hardened will. (Enduring Word: https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-3/; Precept Austin: https://www.preceptaustin.org/ezekiel_31-15)
- **Reformed (Ligonier):** The Jews' essential problem was not that they lacked intellectual capacity to understand Ezekiel’s preaching but that their hard hearts would not believe him. This is why a key theme in Ezekiel is that God must give new hearts to His people (11:14–21; 36:22–27). (https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/scroll-and-watchman)
- **Gill:** Ezekiel was not sent to the Babylonians among whom he dwelt, but to his own people in their native tongue. (https://mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/ezekiel/3.htm)
- **Taylor (quoted by Guzik):** "The words are used to point the contrast between the excusable inability of people of a foreign language to understand and the quite inexcusable stubbornness of Ezekiel’s Israelite hearers." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-3/)

### v. 7 — "But the house of Israel will be unwilling to listen to you, since they are unwilling to listen to Me."

- **Traditional Reading:** The rejection of Ezekiel is ultimately a rejection of God. The people are described as "hard-headed and hard-hearted" (or "impudent and hard-hearted" in older translations). (Enduring Word: https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-3/)
- **Trapp (quoted by Guzik):** "A man’s will is his hell… It is easier to deal with twenty men’s reasons than with one man’s will." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-3/)
- **Wright (quoted by Guzik):** "Ezekiel 3:7 is one of the most dangerous verses in Scripture… It is a call to intense humility, for fear that we comfort ourselves concerning our off-putting presentation of the truth by calling our rejection the rejection of Christ." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-3/)

### vv. 8–9 — "I will make your face as hard as their faces, and your forehead as hard as their foreheads… like a diamond, harder than flint."

- **Traditional Reading:** God matches Ezekiel's constitution to the task. Israel are hard in their rebellion; God makes Ezekiel harder in courage and integrity. The "adamant" stone (diamond) is harder than flint. (Enduring Word: https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-3/)
- **Spurgeon (quoted by Guzik):** "Make your face like adamant if their hearts are like adamant; if they are not ashamed to sin, do not you be ashamed to warn them; if they are not ashamed of their unbelief, be not you ashamed of your faith in the divine testimony." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-3/)
- **McGee (quoted by Guzik):** "God didn’t make Jeremiah’s head hard. Jeremiah had a soft heart, and he couldn’t stand up against all the trouble he faced… Ezekiel is not about to resign." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-3/)
- **Matthew Henry:** Christ promises to strengthen him. He must continue earnest in preaching, whatever the success might be. (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/mhc/ezekiel/3.htm)

### v. 10 — "Listen carefully to all the words I speak to you, and take them to heart."

- **Traditional Reading:** The Hebrew verbs here are imperatives: "take into your heart" (Qal imperative) and "listen closely" (Qal imperative). Before Ezekiel can speak for God, he must receive God's Word deeply into his own heart. (Precept Austin: https://www.preceptaustin.org/ezekiel_31-15)
- **Matthew Henry:** He must speak all that, and that only, which God spoke to him. How can we better speak God's mind than with His words? (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/mhc/ezekiel/3.htm)

### v. 11 — "Go to your people, the exiles… whether they listen or refuse to listen."

- **Traditional Reading:** Ezekiel's proclamation does not depend on the people's reception. His job is to deliver God's message (prefaced by "Thus says the Lord GOD"), not to compel a response. (Enduring Word: https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-3/)
- **Wiersbe (quoted by Guzik):** "It’s a good thing for the servant of God to be among his people, to weep with those who weep and rejoice with those who rejoice, for he can better minister to them when he knows their hearts and feels their pain." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-3/)

### vv. 12–13 — "Then the Spirit lifted me up, and I heard a great rumbling sound… 'Blessed be the glory of the LORD in His dwelling place!'"

- **Traditional Reading:** As the vision of God's chariot-throne begins to withdraw, Ezekiel hears the sound of the living creatures' wings and the wheels — a thunderous noise — and a cry of praise: "Blessed be the glory of the LORD from His place." This phrase has been preserved in Jewish liturgy (the morning service of the Jewish Prayer Book, per Taylor). (Enduring Word: https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-3/)
- **Matthew Henry:** This mission made the holy angels rejoice. All this was to convince Ezekiel that the God who sent him had power to bear him out in his work. (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/mhc/ezekiel/3.htm)
- **Ellicott:** The division between chapters 2 and 3 is unfortunate; both should be read as one continuous passage. What is symbolically described in the last verses of Ezekiel 2 and the first of Ezekiel 3 is expressed plainly in Ezekiel 3:10–11. (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/ezekiel/3.htm)

### v. 14 — "So the Spirit lifted me up and took me away, and I went in bitterness and in the anger of my spirit, with the strong hand of the LORD upon me."

- **Traditional Reading:** The "bitterness" and "heat of spirit" have been variously interpreted. Taylor (quoted by Guzik) says the Hebrew *mar* ("bitter") can express fierce anger, discontentment, or wretchedness. Coupled with "heat of spirit," anger is the dominant emotion — perhaps anger at the sin of the people, the difficulty of his calling, or his own lot as a captive. (Enduring Word: https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-3/)
- **Matthew Henry:** He was overwhelmed with grief for the sins and miseries of his people, and overpowered by the glory of the vision he had seen. (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/mhc/ezekiel/3.htm)
- **Catholic (Haydock, citing Septuagint):** The Septuagint renders it "I went aloft (like a meteor) by the impulse of my spirit; for the hand of the Lord upon me was strong." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/hcc/ezekiel-3.html)
- **Guzik:** "God's word was sweet to Ezekiel (v. 3), but he soon experienced some bitterness in carrying out his call." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-3/)

### v. 15 — "I came to the exiles at Tel-abib… and for seven days I sat where they sat and remained there among them, overwhelmed."

- **Traditional Reading:** "Tel-abib" means "the hill of ears of corn" (Vawter and Hoppe, quoted by Guzik). Ezekiel obeyed God's command to "go, get to the captives" (v. 11). The seven days of stunned silence among the exiles have been compared to the seven-day consecration of a priest (Leviticus 8:33) — a kind of ordination to a prophetic priesthood. (Enduring Word: https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-3/)
- **Peake's Commentary:** The prophet, still under strong divinely produced excitement, came to the community of exiles and after seven days of stupefaction received a further commission. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/pfc/ezekiel-3.html)
- **Matthew Henry:** However retirement, meditation, and communion with God may be sweet, the servant of the Lord must prepare to serve his generation. (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/mhc/ezekiel/3.htm)

### vv. 16–17 — "At the end of seven days… 'Son of man, I have made you a watchman for the house of Israel.'"

- **Traditional Reading:** After seven days, God gives Ezekiel his formal job description: he is a *watchman* (*tsaphah* in Hebrew, *skopos* in the Greek Septuagint). A watchman in the ancient world was a sentinel on city walls tasked with spotting approaching danger and sounding the alarm. If he failed, the blood of the city was on his hands. (Precept Austin: https://www.preceptaustin.org/ezekiel_316-27; Enduring Word: https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-3/)
- **Gill:** The Targum renders "watchman" as "a teacher"; the office is the same as that of bishops or overseers. (https://mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/ezekiel/3.htm)
- **Reformed (Ligonier, citing Calvin):** "What Ezekiel heard belongs to all teachers of the Church, namely, that they are Divinely appointed and placed as on watch-towers, that they may keep watch for the common safety of all." Preachers must always preach the truth, even when it is hard for their congregations to bear. (https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/scroll-and-watchman)
- **Peake's Commentary:** This passage emphasizes the idea of individual responsibility. "For the first time in Hebrew history the prophet becomes a pastor; he has the 'care of souls.'" (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/pfc/ezekiel-3.html)

### v. 18 — "If I say to the wicked man, 'You will surely die,' but you do not warn him… I will hold you responsible for his blood."

- **Traditional Reading:** The principle of "blood-guiltiness" is central. If Ezekiel fails to deliver God's warning, he bears moral responsibility for the sinner's death. The expression "require blood at your hand" is equivalent to requiring the death penalty — the law of retribution. (Precept Austin: https://www.preceptaustin.org/ezekiel_316-27; Enduring Word: https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-3/)
- **Clarke (quoted by Guzik):** A severe warning to ministers: "O what a perdition awaits you! To have the blood of every soul that has died in your parishes… unconverted laid at your door!… Vain your boast of apostolical authority, while ye do not the work of apostles!" (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-3/)
- **Catholic (Haydock):** He (the pastor) kills the man whom he delivers up to death by silence — citing St. Gregory. "If he be damned, though he must blame himself chiefly, yet the blood of his soul shall cry for vengeance more than Abel's." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/hcc/ezekiel-3.html)
- **Death in this context:** Guzik, citing Alexander, notes that "life" and "death" here are primarily physical (covenant curse under Moses), not eternal — though the two often overlap. The false prophets were telling people to resist Babylon, which would lead to physical death; the path of safety was obedient trust in God's judgments. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-3/)

### v. 19 — "But if you warn a wicked man and he does not turn… he will die in his iniquity, but you will have saved yourself."

- **Traditional Reading:** The watchman is responsible for faithful delivery of the message, not for the response. If Ezekiel has warned faithfully, he has "delivered his soul." The people's blood is on their own heads. (Enduring Word: https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-3/; Precept Austin: https://www.preceptaustin.org/ezekiel_316-27)
- **Morgan (quoted by Guzik):** "There is such a thing as blood-guiltiness. If the wicked die in wickedness for lack of the prophetic word, the prophet is guilty of his blood." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-3/)

### v. 20 — "Now if a righteous man turns from his righteousness and commits iniquity, and I put a stumbling block before him, he will die."

- **Traditional Reading:** The watchman's duty extends not only to the openly wicked but also to the ostensibly righteous who may stray. The "stumbling block" does not mean God deliberately trips up the righteous; rather, He leaves opportunities for sin in the paths of men so that if their heart is bent on sin, they earn their own condemnation. (Enduring Word, quoting Taylor: https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-3/)
- **Catholic (Haydock/Worthington):** The "stumbling block before him" is understood as God taking away His grace in punishment of the man's revolt. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/hcc/ezekiel-3.html)
- **His righteous acts will not be remembered:** This underscores that past righteousness does not insulate one from judgment for present sin — a major theme expanded in Ezekiel 18. (Enduring Word: https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-3/)

### v. 21 — "But if you warn the righteous man not to sin, and he does not sin, he will indeed live… and you will have saved yourself."

- **Traditional Reading:** The warning to the righteous is preventative — to keep them on the path. Both the warned righteous person and the faithful watchman are preserved. (Enduring Word: https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-3/)
- **Matthew Henry:** "We are not only to encourage and comfort those who appear to be righteous, but they are to be warned, for many have grown high-minded and secure, have fallen, and even died in their sins." (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/mhc/ezekiel/3.htm)

### vv. 22–23 — "Get up, go out to the plain… the glory of the LORD was present there, like the glory I had seen by the River Kebar, and I fell facedown."

- **Traditional Reading:** This is a third commissioning encounter. The glory of the LORD reappears — the same glory Ezekiel saw in chapter 1 — confirming that the God who called him is still with him. Ezekiel's response is the same: he falls facedown in worship. (Enduring Word: https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-3/)
- **Dummelow:** This third commission was connected with a repetition of the vision, apparently in the neighbourhood of Tel-abib. (https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcb/ezekiel-3.html)

### vv. 24–26 — "Go, shut yourself inside your house… they will tie with ropes… I will make your tongue stick to the roof of your mouth."

- **Traditional Reading:** God imposes an unusual restriction: Ezekiel is to be house-bound and mute except when God specifically opens his mouth. This dramatizes that every prophetic word must come from God alone. The silence is also a sign of judgment on a rebellious people — God withdraws the prophetic voice from them. (Enduring Word: https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-3/)
- **Ellicott:** Until the destruction of Jerusalem, Ezekiel would be greatly restrained in his ordinary utterances by the opposition of the people; yet there would be times when God would give him a message with such power that he would be constrained to declare it. (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/ezekiel/3.htm, see Excursus)
- **Bridgeway Bible Commentary:** Alternatively, Ezekiel may have voluntarily acted dumb and allowed someone to bind him with ropes. When God's time came, he was to go and announce God's message. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/bbc/ezekiel-3.html)
- **Catholic (St. Jerome, cited by Haydock):** "When there is a multitude of sins, the offenders are unworthy of being corrected by the Lord." The prophet's silence itself might suffice to admonish them. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/hcc/ezekiel-3.html)

### v. 27 — "But when I speak with you, I will open your mouth… 'This is what the Lord GOD says.' Whoever listens, let him listen; and whoever refuses, let him refuse."

- **Traditional Reading:** Ezekiel will speak only at God's initiative and only God's words. The final line — "Whoever listens, let him listen; and whoever refuses, let him refuse" — places the responsibility squarely on the hearers. It echoes Jesus' words in the Gospels ("He who has ears to hear, let him hear"). (Enduring Word: https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-3/)
- **Catholic (Calmet, cited by Haydock):** "The man who makes good use of grace shall receive more; but he who despises the offers of God, shall be justly deprived of them in his greatest need." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/hcc/ezekiel-3.html)
- **Matthew Henry:** "When the Lord opened Ezekiel's mouth, he was to deliver his message boldly, to place life and death, the blessing and the curse, before the people, and leave them to their choice." (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/mhc/ezekiel/3.htm)

---

## Notes on Traditions and Distinctive Readings

### Reformed / Presbyterian
- **Ligonier:** Emphasises divine sovereignty in the watchman passage — God appoints the watchman; the hearers' inability to respond is due to hard hearts, pointing to the necessity of God giving new hearts (Ezekiel 11, 36). Calvin is cited directly: the watchman charge "belongs to all teachers of the Church." The sweetness of the scroll of curses is understood through a gospel lens: only after hearing the curse is one ready for the gospel of salvation. (https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/scroll-and-watchman)

### Baptist
- **Spurgeon (quoted in Enduring Word):** On v. 3, he applied the sweetness of the scroll to spiritual appetite: "If the word of God be not very sweet to me, have I an appetite?… When a soul is full of itself, and of the world, and of the pleasures of sin, I do not wonder that it sees no sweetness in Christ, for it has no appetite!" On vv. 8–9, he urged boldness mirroring the people's stubbornness. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-3/)
- **Gill:** Identifies the "watchman" office with that of New Testament bishops/overseers — teachers appointed by Christ, not by themselves, to watch over souls and warn of danger. (https://mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/ezekiel/3.htm)

### Pentecostal / Charismatic
- **Enduring Word (David Guzik):** While broadly evangelical, Guzik's commentary is used across traditions including charismatic circles. His emphasis on the "vision" being a real spiritual experience ("spiritual and divine virtual reality") and the Spirit lifting and transporting the prophet resonates with Pentecostal openness to supernatural encounter. No distinctively Pentecostal interpretation of this chapter was located in the available sources. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-3/)

### Catholic
- **Haydock's Catholic Bible Commentary:** The eating of the scroll signifies devout meditation and interior assimilation of God's Word. On v. 20, the "stumbling block" is understood in terms of God withdrawing grace in punishment of revolt. On vv. 24–26, the prophet's silence is a judgment — when sin abounds, God withholds the corrective voice. On v. 27, the closing phrase is linked to Revelation 22:11 ("He that is unjust, let him be unjust still"), denoting the most desperate condition. St. Gregory and St. Jerome are cited on pastoral responsibility and silence as judgment. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/hcc/ezekiel-3.html)
- **Catholic Encyclopedia:** Ezekiel's name means "strong is God" or "whom God makes strong" (cf. 3:8). His ministry was to foretell God's faithfulness in the midst of trials as well as the fulfilment of His promises. (https://www.newadvent.org/cathen/05737b.htm)

### Modern Scholarship
- **Peake's Commentary:** Notes that for the first time in Hebrew history the prophet becomes a pastor with "care of souls." The watchman passage applies individual responsibility particularly to the calling of the prophet or preacher. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/pfc/ezekiel-3.html)
- **Dummelow:** The commission came in three distinct stages: the first after the initial vision (2:1–3:13), the second seven days later among the exiles (3:14–21), and the third with a repetition of the vision (3:22–27). The eating of the scroll is the basis for Revelation 10:9–10. (https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcb/ezekiel-3.html)
- **Ellicott:** The chapter division is unfortunate; Ezekiel 2–3 should be read as one continuous passage. He also provides an excursus on the figurative language and symbolical actions of Ezekiel, noting that some actions were done in vision only, while others were literal events used symbolically. (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/ezekiel/3.htm)

---

**Sources consulted:** Enduring Word (Guzik), Precept Austin, Matthew Henry (BibleHub), Ellicott (BibleHub), Gill's Exposition (BibleHub/StudyLight), Haydock's Catholic Bible Commentary (StudyLight), Peake's Commentary (StudyLight), Dummelow's Commentary (StudyLight), Bridgeway Bible Commentary (StudyLight), Ligonier Reformed Devotional, Catholic Encyclopedia (New Advent), Benson's Commentary (StudyLight).
